Sic enim prior in chronico, ad annum Christi XLI. “Rediens Jacobus Gallias invisit, ac Britannias, ac Venetiarum oppida, ubi prædicat; ac Hierosolymam revertitur, de rebus gravissimis consulturus beatam Virginem et Petrum.” Posterior, in speculo historiali, (in Basileensi etiam concilio, ab Alphonso Garsia de sancta Maria, Castellani regis oratore, productus) ita: “Apostolis diversa cosmi climata adeuntibus, nutu Dei Jacobus Hiberniæ oris appulsus, verbum Dei prædicavit intrepidus, ubi septem discipulos elegisse fertur: scilicet Torquatum, Secundum, Indalecium, Tisephontem, Eufrasium, Cecilium, Isichium, quorum collogio lolium extirparet, ac telluri aridæ et diu sterili semina verbi Dei committeret. Cumque dies immineret supremus, Hierosolymam cum eis perrexit, ibique martyrium subiit.”
opus_english: Some report — from the book on the sufferings of the martyrs by Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, written in Arabic — that St. James the son of Zebedee, the brother of John, went away into the west and performed many miracles in those regions. Isidore too, in his book on the fathers of both Testaments, records that the same man "preached the Gospel to the peoples of Spain and of the western regions, and poured the light of his preaching into the setting of the world"; and following him, Freculf of Lisieux. The author of the chronicle that circulates under the name of Maximus, bishop of Saragossa, likewise asserts that he "preached on the western shores before all the other apostles." That he preached to the Britons is affirmed by the man who has put on the mask of Flavius Lucius Dexter, and that he preached to the Irish by Vincent of Beauvais. For the former says, in his chronicle, at the year of Christ 41: "On his return James visited Gaul, and the Britains, and the towns of the Veneti, where he preaches; and he returns to Jerusalem to consult the blessed Virgin and Peter on matters of the gravest importance." The latter, in his "Speculum Historiale" (and cited also at the Council of Basel by Alfonso García de Santa María, ambassador of the king of Castile), writes thus: "While the apostles were going to the various regions of the world, James, by the will of God, having landed on the shores of Ireland, fearlessly preached the word of God, where he is said to have chosen seven disciples: namely Torquatus, Secundus, Indaletius, Tisephon, Euphrasius, Caecilius, and Hesychius, that by their fellowship he might root out the tares and commit the seeds of the word of God to the dry and long-barren earth. And when his last day drew near, he went on with them to Jerusalem, and there underwent martyrdom."
gemini_english: Certain writers record from the book of Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, written in Arabic concerning the sufferings of the martyrs, that St. James the son of Zebedee, the brother of John, departed into the west, and performed many miracles in those places. Isidore also relates in his book "*On the Fathers of Both Testaments*" that this same man "preached the gospel to the peoples of Spain and the western regions, and poured the light of his preaching into the setting of the world," and Freculf of Lisieux follows him; the author of the chronicle which is circulated under the name of Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza, also asserts that he "preached first of all the apostles in the western coasts." He who put on the mask of Flavius Lucius Dexter affirms that he preached to the Britons, while Vincent of Beauvais affirms that he preached to the Irish. For thus the former says in his chronicle, at the year of Christ 41: "Returning, James visits the Gauls, and the Britains, and the towns of the Venetians, where he preaches; and he returns to Jerusalem, to consult the Blessed Virgin and Peter concerning the most weighty matters." The latter, in his "*Historical Mirror*" (produced also at the Council of Basel by Alfonso Garcia de Santa Maria, the ambassador of the king of Castile), speaks thus: "As the apostles were approaching the diverse climates of the world, James, driven to the coasts of Ireland by the will of God, intrepidly preached the word of God, where he is said to have chosen seven disciples: namely Torquatus, Secundus, Indalecius, Ctesiphon, Euphrasius, Caecilius, and Hesychius, by whose fellowship he might extirpate the tares, and commit the seeds of the word of God to an arid and long-sterile earth. And when his final day was imminent, he proceeded with them to Jerusalem, and there underwent martyrdom."

latin: Nam quum temporum plenitudo advenisset, “mysterium quod a temporibus seculorum tacitum fuit, factum est manifestum, et per Scripturas propheticas ex imperio æterni Dei ad obedientiam fidei omnibus gentibus declaratum.” Indeque iis qui in tenebris et umbra mortis erant positi, lumen illud gentibus patefaciendum aﬀulsit: de quo apud prophetam Deus; “Constitui te ut sis lux gentium, ut sis saluti usque ad ﬁnes terræ.” Christo enim apostolis suis imperante, ut profecti in mundum universum, prædicarent evangelium omni creaturæ; egressi illi prædicarunt ubique, ita ut nullum locum cœlesti doctrinæ occultum esse sinerent; “μὴ νήσους, μὴ ἤπειρον, μηδ' εἴτινα τρίτην ἀνθρώποις κατοικίαν ἡ φύσις ἐδίδου, non insulas, non continentem, non si quam tertiam habitationem hominibus natura concessit:” quemadmodum Gregorius Nyssenus loquitur. Atque ita completum est quod per Esaiam olim Deus prædixerat: “Mittam ex eis ad gentes in oceano, insulasque remotissimas, quæ non audiverant famam meam, neque viderant gloriam meam, ut indicent gloriam meam in gentibus.” Nam “verbum Dei,” Augustini verba hæc sunt, “non in sola continenti terra prædicatum est; sed etiam in insulis, quæ constitutæ sunt in medio mari: et ipsæ plenæ Christianis, plenæ sunt servis Dei. Non enim separat mare eum, qui fecerat mare.
opus_english: For when the fullness of time had come, “the mystery which had been kept silent from the times of the ages was made manifest, and through the prophetic Scriptures, by the command of the eternal God, was declared to all peoples for the obedience of faith.” And from this that light, destined to be revealed to the peoples, shone upon those who were set in darkness and the shadow of death: concerning which God speaks through the prophet, “I have appointed you to be a light to the peoples, that you may be for salvation to the ends of the earth.” For when Christ commanded his apostles to go out into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature, they went out and preached everywhere, so that they allowed no place to remain hidden from the heavenly doctrine; “μὴ νήσους, μὴ ἤπειρον, μηδ' εἴτινα τρίτην ἀνθρώποις κατοικίαν ἡ φύσις ἐδίδου [neither the islands, nor the mainland, nor any third dwelling-place that nature had granted to humankind],” as Gregory of Nyssa puts it. And thus was fulfilled what God had once foretold through Isaiah: “I will send some of them to the peoples in the ocean, and to the most remote islands, which had not heard my fame nor seen my glory, that they may declare my glory among the peoples.” For “the word of God,” — these are Augustine’s words — “has been preached not on the continental land alone, but also in the islands, which are set in the midst of the sea: and these too are full of Christians, full of the servants of God. For the sea does not separate them from him who had made the sea.”
gemini_english: For when the fullness of time had come, "the mystery which was kept secret for long ages has been made manifest, and through the prophetic Scriptures, by the command of the eternal God, has been made known to all peoples for the obedience of faith." And thence upon those who were placed in darkness and the shadow of death, that light to be revealed to the peoples shone forth: concerning which God says in the prophet, "I have appointed you to be a light to the peoples, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth." For when Christ commanded his apostles that, having set out into the whole world, they should preach the gospel to every creature; they went forth and preached everywhere, so that they allowed no place to be hidden from heavenly doctrine; "μὴ νήσους, μὴ ἤπειρον, μηδ' εἴτινα τρίτην ἀνθρώποις κατοικίαν ἡ φύσις ἐδίδου [not islands, not the continent, nor if nature has granted any third habitation to men]:" as Gregory of Nyssa says. And thus was fulfilled what God had formerly foretold through Isaiah: "I will send from them to the peoples in the ocean, and to the most remote islands, which had not heard my fame, nor seen my glory, that they may declare my glory among the peoples." For "the word of God," these are the words of Augustine, "was preached not only on the continental land; but also in the islands, which are situated in the middle of the sea: and they themselves are full of Christians, they are full of the servants of God. latin: PRISCÆ illius ignorantiæ temporibus, quæ salutarem Christi adventum præcesserunt, Britannos et Hibernos nostros communem reliquarum gentium sortem subiisse, id est, “fuisse absque Christo, alienos a republica Israelis, et extraneos quod ad fœdera promissionis attinet, spem non habentes, et sine Deo in mundo:” non est quod quisquam dubitet. “Neque enim Britannia fertilis provincia tyrannorum,” inquiebat olim impius Porphyrius, “et Scoticæ gentes omnesque usque ad oceanum per circuitum barbaræ nationes Moysen prophetasque cognoverant.” Neque minus falluntur viri docti, qui Britannos a Druydibus suis in unius Dei cultu semper institutos fuisse tradunt, quam nugatus est Postellus, quum ab Hebræis Hibernorum originem conatus est arcessere. Nam et Origenes, quem illi authorem citant, plane contrarium indicat, “terram Britanniæ ante adventum Christi in unius dei religionem” minime consensisse: nominatim vero Andrasten sive Andaten, Victoriæ deam, Dio Cassius, Apollinem et Dianam alii a Britannis coli consuevisse prodiderunt: et de eorum idolomania gentilis ipsorum Gildas tam clarum perhibet testimonium, ut res in quæstionem vocari non debeat. Sic enim ille: “Igitur omittens priscos illos communesquc cum omnibus gentibus errores, quibus ante adventum Christi in carne omne humanum genus obligabatur adstrictum; nec enumerans patriæ portenta ipsa diabolica, pene numero Egyptiaca vincentia, quorum nonnulla lineamentis adhuc deformibus intra vel extra deserta mœnia, solito more rigentia torvis vultibus intuemur: neque nominatim inclamitans montes ipsos, aut colles, vel fluvios, olim exitiales, nunc vero humanis usibus utiles, quibus divinus honor a cæco tunc populo cumulabatur, &c.” Ut de illorum temporum miserrima, et subsequentium felicissima conditione, in epitaphio Nepotiani B. Hieronymus pronuntiare non dubitaverit. “Ubi tunc totius orbis homines, ab India usque ad Britanniam, a rigida septentrionis plaga usque ad fervores Atlantici oceani tam innumerabiles populi, et tantarum gentium multitudines; Quam variæ linguis, habitu tam vestis et armis?
opus_english: No one need doubt that, in those times of ancient ignorance which preceded the saving advent of Christ, our Britons and Irish underwent the common lot of the other nations — that is, that they were “without Christ, aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers as regards the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.” For, as the impious Porphyry once said, “neither had Britain, a province fertile in tyrants, nor the Scottish peoples and all the barbarous nations round about as far as the ocean, known Moses and the prophets.” Nor are the learned men who maintain that the Britons were always instructed by their Druids in the worship of one God any less mistaken than Postel was when he trifled in attempting to derive the origin of the Irish from the Hebrews. For even Origen, whom they cite as their authority, indicates plainly the contrary — that “the land of Britain, before the advent of Christ, by no means agreed in the religion of one God”; and specifically Dio Cassius has recorded that Andraste, or Andate, the goddess of Victory, and others that Apollo and Diana, were customarily worshipped by the Britons; and concerning their idol-madness their own countryman Gildas furnishes so clear a testimony that the matter ought not to be called into question. For thus he writes: “Therefore, passing over those ancient errors, common to all the nations, by which the whole human race was bound fast before the advent of Christ in the flesh; and not enumerating the diabolical monstrosities of my country, almost exceeding in number those of Egypt, some of which we still behold, with their features yet misshapen, within or without the deserted walls, rigid after the usual manner with their grim countenances; nor crying out by name against the very mountains, or hills, or rivers, once deadly but now useful for human purposes, upon which divine honour was then heaped by a blind people, &c.” So that the blessed Jerome, in his epitaph of Nepotian, did not hesitate to pronounce upon the most wretched condition of those times and the most happy condition of those that followed: “Where then were the men of the whole world, from India even to Britain, from the rigid region of the north even to the heats of the Atlantic ocean — peoples so innumerable, and multitudes of nations so great; how varied in their tongues, how varied in the fashion of their dress and their arms?”
gemini_english: No one should doubt that in the times of that ancient ignorance which preceded the saving advent of Christ, our Britons and Irish suffered the common lot of the rest of the nations, that is, "they were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world." "For neither Britain, a province fertile in tyrants," as the impious Porphyry once said, "nor the Scottish peoples, nor all the barbarous nations round about as far as the ocean, had known Moses and the prophets." And learned men who relate that the Britons were always instructed by their Druids in the worship of one God are no less mistaken than Postel was when he attempted to derive the origin of the Irish from the Hebrews. For Origen, whom they cite as an authority, indicates the exact opposite, that "the land of Britain before the advent of Christ" did not consent "to the religion of one God": but Dio Cassius specifically recorded that Andraste or Andate, the goddess of Victory, and others recorded that Apollo and Diana, were customarily worshipped by the Britons; and their own countryman Gildas provides such clear testimony concerning their idolatry that the matter ought not to be called into question. For he speaks thus: "Therefore, omitting those ancient errors common to all nations, by which all the human race was bound fast before the advent of Christ in the flesh; and not enumerating the diabolical monstrosities of my country, almost surpassing the Egyptian in number, some of which we still see with their deformed features within or without deserted walls, stiff with fierce expressions in their usual manner; nor specifically crying out against the mountains themselves, or the hills, or the rivers, once deadly but now useful for human needs, upon which divine honor was heaped by a then blind people, etc." So that Jerome did not hesitate to declare concerning the most wretched condition of those times, and the most happy condition of the subsequent ones, in the epitaph of Nepotian: "Where then were the men of the whole world, from India even to Britain, from the freezing region of the north even to the heat of the Atlantic ocean, such innumerable peoples, and multitudes of such great nations; however varied in languages, and in the style of their dress and arms?"

Our own writers gather from the poet Martial that Claudia was British by nationality and the wife of Pudens; for he sang of Claudia thus: Although Claudia Rufina is sprung from the woad-blue Britons, why does she possess the heart of the Latin people?
gemini_english: But the Liber Pontificalis asserts that the father of Linus was a certain Herculanus. Our writers gather from the poet Martial that Claudia was British by nation, and the wife of Pudens: who sang thus of Claudia: Since Claudia Rufina is sprung from the blue Britons, why does she hold the hearts of the Latin people?

latin: Et ita sane in martyrologio Romano (quod Hieronymi nomine olim editum, supposita quoque ejusdem ad Chromatium et Heliodorum epistola, confirmat Baronius) ut et in Bedæ, Usuardi, Notkeri et Adonis martyrologiis, ad Idus Maii, legimus; “ Romæ hos a sanctis apostolis episcopos ordinatos, et ad prædicandum verbum Dei in Hispanias directos esse: cumque diversis urbibus evangelizassent, et innumeras multitudines Christi fidei subjugassent ;” tandem in dictis Hispaniæ locis quievisse. In vetere Romanæ Ecclesiæ martyrologio, quod suo præfixit Ado, non aliud de illis dicitur, quam quod “ Romæ ab apostolis ordinati sunt.” In Britannico vero, quod describendum curavit Ricemarchus Sulgeni Menevensis episcopi filius, ne nominantur quidem. In apostolorum tamen catalogo, qui epistolæ ad Chromatium et Heliodorum ibi subjicitur, de Jacobo legitur: “ Hic Hispaniæ, et in occidentalia loca prædicavit: et sub Herode gladio cæsus occubuit.” Addit Ordericus Vitalis Uticensis monachus, libro secundo ecclesiasticæ historiæ, septem ipsius discipulos cadaver ejus in Hispaniam detulisse, “ et a rege Galliciæ susceptos, primum fidem et religionem Hiberis prædicavisse.” An pro Hiberis Vincentius alicubi Hibernis exaratum repererit, aliis conjiciendum relinquo : certe hujusmodi aliquo errore dictos Jacobi discipulos ad Hiberniam translatos esse, a vero non est absimile.
opus_english: And so indeed in the Roman Martyrology (which Baronius confirms was once published under Jerome's name, together with a likewise supposititious letter of the same Jerome to Chromatius and Heliodorus), as also in the martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Notker, and Ado, at the Ides of May, we read that “these men were ordained bishops at Rome by the holy apostles, and were sent into Spain to preach the word of God; and when they had evangelized in various cities, and had brought countless multitudes under the faith of Christ,” they at last rested in the said places of Spain. In the old martyrology of the Roman Church, which Ado prefixed to his own, nothing else is said of them than that “they were ordained at Rome by the apostles.” But in the British martyrology, which Ricemarchus, son of Sulgenus bishop of Menevia, saw to be transcribed, they are not even named. Yet in the catalogue of the apostles, which is there appended to the letter to Chromatius and Heliodorus, it is recorded of James: “He preached to Spain and to the western regions, and under Herod he fell, slain by the sword.” Orderic Vitalis, the monk of Ouche, adds, in the second book of his Ecclesiastical History, that seven of his disciples carried his body into Spain, “and, being received by the king of Galicia, first preached the faith and religion to the Iberians.” Whether Vincent somewhere found “Hiberni” (the Irish) written in place of “Hiberi” (the Iberians), I leave for others to conjecture; certainly it is not far from the truth that, through some error of this kind, the said disciples of James were transferred to Ireland.
gemini_english: And indeed I read thus in the Roman martyrology (which Baronius confirms was formerly published under the name of Jerome, with a forged epistle of his to Chromatius and Heliodorus also appended), as also in the martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Notker, and Ado, at the Ides of May: 'that these were ordained bishops at Rome by the holy apostles, and directed to Spain to preach the word of God: and when they had evangelized in various cities, and subjected countless multitudes to the faith of Christ,' they at length rested in the said places of Spain. In the old martyrology of the Roman Church, which Ado prefixed to his own, nothing else is said of them than that 'they were ordained at Rome by the apostles.' But in the British one, which Ricemarchus, son of Sulgenus, bishop of Menevia, had copied, they are not even named. However, in the catalogue of the apostles, which is there appended to the epistle to Chromatius and Heliodorus, it is read concerning James: 'He preached to Spain and the western places: and fell, slain by the sword under Herod.' Orderic Vitalis, a monk of Uticum, adds in the second book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, that seven of his disciples brought his corpse to Spain, 'and having been received by the king of Galicia, first preached the faith and religion to the Iberians.' Whether Vincent somewhere found 'Hibernians' written instead of 'Iberians', I leave to others to conjecture: certainly it is quite likely that by some error of this kind the said disciples of James were transferred to Ireland.

latin: "Quod profecto divina providentia ita tunc Cæsaris sensibus ingessit, ut absque ullo obstaculo, in ipsis duntaxat initiis Evangelii sermo usquequaque percurreret. Unde et factum est, ut repente quasi cœlitus lumen ostensum, aut radius quidam solis erumpens, totum orbem claritate superni luminis illustraret: ut compleretur illa prophetia quæ dixerat, In omnem terram exivit sonus eorum, evangelistarum scilicet et apostolorum, et in fines orbis terræ verba eorum. Ex quo et per omnes civitates ac vicos, immensæ multitudines, velut messium tempore frumenta ad areas, ita ad Ecclesias populi congregabantur." "Congregatio Christianorum in omne hominum penetravit genus; nec ulla natio Romani orbis remansit, quæ cultus ejus expers relinqueretur." Μία ἡ ἐκκλησία, ἣν ἱδρύσαντο οἱ ἅγιοι ἀπόστολοι ἀπὸ περάτων ἕως περάτων ἐν τῷ αἵματι τοῦ Χριστοῦ, οἰκείοις ἱδρῶσι καὶ πόνοις.
opus_english: "This indeed divine providence then so impressed upon Caesar's mind that, without any obstacle, at the very outset of the Gospel the word might run everywhere in every direction. Hence it also came about that suddenly, as though a light shown from heaven or a certain ray of the sun bursting forth, illumined the whole world with the brightness of that light from on high: so that the prophecy might be fulfilled which had said, 'Their sound went out into all the earth' — that is, the sound of the evangelists and apostles — 'and their words to the ends of the world.' From this, throughout all cities and villages, immense multitudes were gathered to the Churches as a people, just as grain is brought to the threshing floors at harvest time." "The fellowship of the Christians penetrated every kind of human being; nor did any nation of the Roman world remain that was left without share in its worship." Μία ἡ ἐκκλησία, ἣν ἱδρύσαντο οἱ ἅγιοι ἀπόστολοι ἀπὸ περάτων ἕως περάτων ἐν τῷ αἵματι τοῦ Χριστοῦ, οἰκείοις ἱδρῶσι καὶ πόνοις. [There is one Church, which the holy apostles established from one end of the earth to the other in the blood of Christ, by their own sweat and toil.]
gemini_english: "Divine providence surely instilled this into Caesar's mind at that time, so that without any obstacle, at the very beginnings of the Gospel, its word might run everywhere. Whence it also happened that, suddenly, like a light shown from heaven, or a ray of the sun breaking forth, it illuminated the whole world with the brightness of supernal light: so that the prophecy might be fulfilled which had said, Their sound has gone out into all the earth (namely, that of the evangelists and apostles), and their words to the ends of the earth. From this time, through all cities and villages, immense multitudes were gathered to the churches, just as grain is gathered to the threshing floors at harvest time." latin: Similiter et apud Dorotheum in synopsi, Aristobulum episcopum Britanniæ factum fuisse legimus : et in fragmento, quod Helecæ Cæsaraugustani episcopi nomine habetur editum : " Britannis celebris est memoria multorum martyrum, præcipue S. Aristobuli unius de LXXII. discipulis, qui dictus est etiam Zebedæus (Pater Jacobi, et Joannis martyris, Mariæ Salome) qui cum Petro Romam petivit. Inde relictis domesticis suis, missus in Angliam episcopus, occubuit martyr in secundo anno imperatoris Neronis sævissimi." Ita enim pagina 108. editionis Cæsaraugustanæ habetur. Verum quæ parenthesi inclusimus, sic sunt corrigenda : " Pater Jacobi et Joannis, maritus Mariæ Salomes." In sequente enim pagina, Concordia Petri apostoli uxor, Aristobuli et Salomes filia fuisse perhibetur. " S. Petrus," inquit author, " in honore habetur in Hispaniis, et ejus uxor Concordia passa Romæ sub Nerone, non multo prius quam ipse pateretur. Fuit hæc, ut docet M. Maximus in commentariis ad epistolam S. Petri, filia Aristobuli vel Zebedæi, et Salomes; socrus etiam Andreæ, qui duxit alteram sororem Concordiæ, et Jacobi et Joannis. Fuit autem Aristobulus cognomento Zebedæus, frater Barnabæ apostoli Domini." Hæc ille : cui de Petro, ducente in uxorem filiam Aristobuli, fratris Barnabæ apostoli, astipulantur etiam Græci apud Metaphrastam in commentario de Petro et Paulo, et in Menæis, ad XXIX. Junii diem.
opus_english: Similarly, in Dorotheus's Synopsis as well, we read that Aristobulus was made bishop of Britain; and in the fragment which is published under the name of Heleca, bishop of Saragossa: "Among the Britons the memory of many martyrs is celebrated, especially of St. Aristobulus, one of the seventy-two disciples, who was also called Zebedee (father of James, and of John the martyr, of Mary Salome), who went to Rome with Peter. Then, leaving his household behind, sent into England as bishop, he died a martyr in the second year of the most savage emperor Nero." For so it stands on page 108 of the Saragossa edition. But what I enclosed in the parenthesis must be corrected thus: "Father of James and John, husband of Mary Salome." For on the following page Concordia, the wife of the apostle Peter, is reported to have been the daughter of Aristobulus and Salome. "St. Peter," says the author, "is held in honour in Spain, and his wife Concordia suffered at Rome under Nero, not long before he himself suffered. She was, as M. Maximus teaches in his commentaries on the epistle of St. Peter, the daughter of Aristobulus, or Zebedee, and of Salome; and the mother-in-law also of Andrew, who married another sister of Concordia and of James and John. Now Aristobulus, surnamed Zebedee, was the brother of Barnabas, the apostle of the Lord." Thus he writes; and with him, concerning Peter's taking to wife the daughter of Aristobulus, the brother of the apostle Barnabas, the Greeks too agree — in Metaphrastes, in his commentary on Peter and Paul, and in the Menaia, under the day of June 29.
gemini_english: Similarly, in Dorotheus in his synopsis, I read that Aristobulus was made bishop of Britain: and in a fragment which is published under the name of Heleca, bishop of Zaragoza: "The memory of many martyrs is celebrated among the Britons, especially St. Aristobulus, one of the seventy-two disciples, who was also called Zebedee (the father of James, and of John the martyr, of Mary Salome) who went to Rome with Peter. From there, having left his household, he was sent to England as bishop, and fell as a martyr in the second year of the most cruel emperor Nero." For so it is found on page 108 of the Zaragoza edition. But what I have enclosed in parentheses should be corrected as follows: "The father of James and John, the husband of Mary Salome." For on the following page, Concordia, the wife of the apostle Peter, is said to have been the daughter of Aristobulus and Salome. "St. Peter," says the author, "is held in honor in Spain, and his wife Concordia suffered at Rome under Nero, not much before he himself suffered. She was, as M. Maximus teaches in his commentaries on the epistle of St. Peter, the daughter of Aristobulus or Zebedee, and of Salome; also the mother-in-law of Andrew, who married the other sister of Concordia, and of James and John. Moreover, Aristobulus, surnamed Zebedee, was the brother of Barnabas, the apostle of the Lord." Thus he writes: with whom the Greeks in Metaphrastes in his commentary on Peter and Paul, and in the Menaea, on the 29th day of June, also agree concerning Peter marrying the daughter of Aristobulus, the brother of the apostle Barnabas.

latin: Et Sophronius patriarcha Hierosolymitanus, in sermone de natali apostolorum, Paulum Hispanis et Britannis evangelium prædicasse significat: quod tamen ex aliorum fide refero, mihi enim ipsi auctorem videre nondum contigit. Denique “ tanquam cœlestis quædam volucris orbem habitabilem circumcirca peragrans; triginta et quinque annis evangelico pro Christo certamine peracto,” ut scribit Nicephorus, Romæ demum sub Nerone martyrio cursum consummavit.
opus_english: And Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, in his sermon on the feast of the apostles, indicates that Paul preached the gospel to the Spaniards and the Britons; this, however, I report on the credit of others, for I have not yet myself managed to see the source. The old translator of Chrysostom's sermon on Pentecost likewise hints that he ran from Spain "to the farthest parts" of the earth. Finally, "like some heavenly bird traversing the whole habitable world round about, his evangelical contest for Christ accomplished over thirty-five years," as Nicephorus writes, he at last completed his course by martyrdom at Rome under Nero.

latin: Simonem Petrum, “ duodecim quidem annos esse versatum in oriente, viginti autem et tres annos transegisse Romæ, et in Britannia, et in civitatibus quæ sunt in occidente,” retulit alicubi Eusebius Pamphili; siquidem Simeoni Metaphrastæ credimus. Apud quem etiam legimus, Petrum in Britannia “ longo tempore fuisse moratum, et multas gentes non nominatas attraxisse ad fidem Christi;” ad extremum vero, cum “ verbo gratiæ multos illuminasset, et ecclesias constituisset, episcopos et presbyteros et diaconos ordinasset, XII. anno Cæsaris Neronis rursus Romam reversam esse.”
opus_english: Eusebius Pamphili reports somewhere that Simon Peter “spent twelve years in the East, but passed twenty-three years at Rome, and in Britain, and in the cities which lie in the West”—if indeed Simeon Metaphrastes is to be believed; for in him I also read that Peter “remained a long time in Britain, and drew many unnamed peoples to the faith of Christ,” but at the last, when he had “enlightened many by the word of grace, and established churches, and ordained bishops and presbyters and deacons, in the twelfth year of Caesar Nero returned again to Rome.”
gemini_english: Eusebius of Caesarea recorded somewhere that Simon Peter "spent twelve years in the East, but passed twenty-three years at Rome, and in Britain, and in the cities which are in the West," if indeed I believe Simeon Metaphrastes. latin: S. PAULUM doctorem Gentium τὸν τὴν οἰκουμένην σταδεύσαντα, καὶ τῷ περὶ πίστεως δρόμῳ τὸν κόσμον μικρὸν ἀποφήναντα, (ut de eo loquitur Basilius Seleuciensis) “ ab oceano usque ad oceanum cucurrisse,” affirmat Hieronymus: “ imitantem Dominum suum et solem justitiæ, de quo legimus; A summo cælo egressio ejus, et occursus ejus, usque ad summum ejus, ut ante eum terra deficeret quam studium prædicandi:” et post primam apologiam, cujus ipse in posteriore ad Timotheum epistola meminit, a Nerone dimissum, evangelium Christi in occidentis quoque partibus prædicavisse. Verba apostoli sunt : “ In prima mea defensione nemo mihi adfuit; sed omnes me dereliqueruut. Non illis imputetur. Dominus autem mihi adstitit, et confortavit; ut per me prædicatio impleatur, et audiant omnes gentes.” In quem locum Theodoretus: “ Quando,” inquit, “ appellatione usus, Romam a Festo missus est, defensione audita fuit absolutus, et in Hispaniam profectus est, et ad alias gentes excurrens, eis doctrinæ lucem attulit;” atque, ut alibi addit idem, “ Insulis quæ in mari jacent, utilitatem attulit.” Unde de eo Venantius Fortunatus : Transiit Oceanum, vel qua facit insula portum, Quasque Britannus habet terras, quasque ultima Thule.
opus_english: Jerome affirms that St. Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, τὸν τὴν οἰκουμένην σταδεύσαντα, καὶ τῷ περὶ πίστεως δρόμῳ τὸν κόσμον μικρὸν ἀποφήναντα [who traversed the inhabited world, and by his race for the faith made the world seem small] (as Basil of Seleucia speaks of him), "ran from ocean to ocean," "imitating his Lord and the sun of righteousness, of whom we read: His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit reaches to the highest part of it, so that the earth would sooner fail than his zeal for preaching"; and that, after his first defense — which he himself mentions in the later epistle to Timothy — having been released by Nero, he preached the gospel of Christ in the regions of the West as well. The words of the apostle are: "At my first defense no one stood with me, but all forsook me. May it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled, and all the Gentiles might hear." On which passage Theodoret says: "When," he says, "having made his appeal, he was sent from Festus to Rome, his defense was heard and he was acquitted, and he set out for Spain, and, running out to other peoples, brought them the light of doctrine"; and, as the same author adds elsewhere, "He brought benefit to the islands that lie in the sea." Whence Venantius Fortunatus says of him: He crossed the Ocean, even where the island makes a harbor, and the lands the Briton holds, and those of farthest Thule.
gemini_english: Jerome affirms that St. Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, τὸν τὴν οἰκουμένην σταδεύσαντα, καὶ τῷ περὶ πίστεως δρόμῳ τὸν κόσμον μικρὸν ἀποφήναντα [who ran the race of the inhabited world, and by his course of faith showed the world to be small] (as Basil of Seleucia speaks of him), "ran from ocean to ocean," "imitating his Lord and the sun of justice, of whom we read: 'His going out is from the end of heaven, and his circuit unto the ends of it,' so that the earth would fail before him sooner than his zeal for preaching:" and that after his first defense, which he himself mentions in his second epistle to Timothy, having been released by Nero, he preached the gospel of Christ in the western parts as well. The words of the apostle are: "At my first defense no one stood with me, but all forsook me. May it not be laid to their charge. But the Lord stood with me and strengthened me, that through me the preaching might be fulfilled, and that all the Gentiles might hear." On this passage Theodoret says: "When, having appealed, he was sent to Rome by Festus, he was acquitted after his defense was heard, and he set out for Spain, and running out to other nations, he brought the light of doctrine to them;" and, as the same author adds elsewhere, "He brought benefit to the islands that lie in the sea." Whence Venantius Fortunatus says of him: "He crossed the Ocean, and wherever an island makes a port, and the lands which the Briton holds, and farthest Thule."

opus_english: CHAPTER I. The Britons idolaters before they received the Christian faith. gemini_english: CHAPTER I. The Britons were idolaters before receiving the Christian faith. Concerning the apostles who are said to have first preached the gospel in the British isles: James the son of Zebedee, Simon the Zealot, Simon Peter, and St. Paul. Also concerning Aristobulus, and Claudia the Briton.

latin: Aristobulum quoque cujus ipse in epistola ad Romanos meminit, Britannorum episcopum a Paulo ordinatum, in Menæis Græcorum invenio: ubi Aristobuli ad decimum quintum diem Martii, hujusmodi fit commemoratio: “ Οὗτος ἦν εἷς τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα μαθητῶν, ἠκολούθησε δὲ τῷ ἁγίῳ ἀποστόλῳ Παύλῳ, κηρύττων τὸ εὐαγγέλιον εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην διακονῶν αὐτῷ· ὑφ᾽ οὗ καὶ χειροτονεῖται ἐπίσκοπος εἰς τὴν τῶν Βρετανῶν χώραν, ἀγρίων ἀνδρῶν καὶ ὠμοτάτων· παρ᾽ ὧν ποτὲ μὲν τυπτόμενος, ποτὲ δὲ καὶ κατὰ τῆς ἀγορᾶς συρόμενος, πολλοὺς ἔπεισε τῷ Χριστῷ προσελθεῖν· ὅθεν καὶ ἐκκλησίας συστησάμενος, καὶ πρεσβυτέρους καὶ διακόνους ἐν αὐτῇ καταστήσας, ἐτελειώθη. E septuaginta discipulis erat hic unus, sequutus est autem S. Paulum, prædicans evangelium, et ubique terrarum ministrans illi. A quo et episcopus ordinatus est in Britannorum regionem, ferorum et sævissimorum hominum. A quibus aliquando quidem verberibus affectus, aliquando etiam per forum tractus, multis persuasit ut Christo se adjungerent. Unde et ecclesiis constitutis, et presbyteris et diaconis in ea ordinatis, vitam consummavit."
opus_english: I also find, in the Menaia of the Greeks, that Aristobulus — whom he (Paul) himself mentions in his Epistle to the Romans — was ordained by Paul as a bishop of the Britons: for there, on the fifteenth day of March, a commemoration of Aristobulus is made in these terms: “Οὗτος ἦν εἷς τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα μαθητῶν, ἠκολούθησε δὲ τῷ ἁγίῳ ἀποστόλῳ Παύλῳ, κηρύττων τὸ εὐαγγέλιον εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην διακονῶν αὐτῷ· ὑφ᾽ οὗ καὶ χειροτονεῖται ἐπίσκοπος εἰς τὴν τῶν Βρετανῶν χώραν, ἀγρίων ἀνδρῶν καὶ ὠμοτάτων· παρ᾽ ὧν ποτὲ μὲν τυπτόμενος, ποτὲ δὲ καὶ κατὰ τῆς ἀγορᾶς συρόμενος, πολλοὺς ἔπεισε τῷ Χριστῷ προσελθεῖν· ὅθεν καὶ ἐκκλησίας συστησάμενος, καὶ πρεσβυτέρους καὶ διακόνους ἐν αὐτῇ καταστήσας, ἐτελειώθη [This man was one of the seventy disciples, and he followed the holy apostle Paul, preaching the gospel throughout the whole world and ministering to him; by whom he was also ordained bishop in the region of the Britons, a fierce and most savage people; by them he was at one time beaten, at another even dragged through the marketplace, yet he persuaded many to come to Christ; whence, having established churches and ordained presbyters and deacons in them, he completed his life].”
gemini_english: I also find in the Greek Menaia that Aristobulus, whom he himself mentions in the Epistle to the Romans, was ordained bishop of the Britons by Paul: where, on the fifteenth day of March, a commemoration of Aristobulus is made to this effect: “Οὗτος ἦν εἷς τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα μαθητῶν, ἠκολούθησε δὲ τῷ ἁγίῳ ἀποστόλῳ Παύλῳ, κηρύττων τὸ εὐαγγέλιον εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην διακονῶν αὐτῷ· ὑφ᾽ οὗ καὶ χειροτονεῖται ἐπίσκοπος εἰς τὴν τῶν Βρετανῶν χώραν, ἀγρίων ἀνδρῶν καὶ ὠμοτάτων· παρ᾽ ὧν ποτὲ μὲν τυπτόμενος, ποτὲ δὲ καὶ κατὰ τῆς ἀγορᾶς συρόμενος, πολλοὺς ἔπεισε τῷ Χριστῷ προσελθεῖν· ὅθεν καὶ ἐκκλησίας συστησάμενος, καὶ πρεσβυτέρους καὶ διακόνους ἐν αὐτῇ καταστήσας, ἐτελειώθη [He was one of the seventy disciples, and he followed the holy apostle Paul, preaching the gospel throughout the whole world and ministering to him; by whom he was also ordained bishop for the region of the Britons, a fierce and most savage people; by whom being sometimes beaten, and sometimes dragged through the marketplace, he persuaded many to come to Christ; whence, having established churches and ordained presbyters and deacons in them, he completed his life]."

latin: Πᾶσαν σχεδὸν τὴν γῆν διελθὼν, καὶ ἐπὶ πέντε καὶ τριάκοντα ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ διαθλεύσας ἐνιαυτοῖς. Niceph. hist. eccles. lib. 12. cap. 34. Vix triginta annorum spatio et Romanos, et Persas, et Parthos, et Medos, et Indos, et Scythas, et Sauromatas, et Sarracenos, et omne prorsus humanum genus sub jugum mitteret veritatis, &c. Chrysost. homil. 4. de laudib. Pauli. Clemens in epistola ad Corinthios pag. 8. de eodem: Κῆρυξ γενόμενος ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ καὶ ἐν τῇ δύσει, τὸ γενναῖον τῆς πίστεως αὑτοῦ κλέος ἔλαβεν δικαιοσύνην διδάξαι ὅλον τὸν κόσμον, καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ τέρμα τῆς δύσεως ἐλθὼν, καὶ μαρτυρήσας ἐπὶ τῶν ἡγουμένων, οὕτως ἀπηλλάγη τοῦ κόσμου. In oriente ac occidente verbi præco factus, illustrem fidei suæ fainam sortitus est, in justitia mundum universum instruens, et ad occidentis terminos veniens, et sub imperatoribus martyrium subiens, sic e mundo migravit.
opus_english: Πᾶσαν σχεδὸν τὴν γῆν διελθὼν, καὶ ἐπὶ πέντε καὶ τριάκοντα ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ διαθλεύσας ἐνιαυτοῖς [Having traversed almost the whole earth, and having contended for the gospel on behalf of Christ for thirty-five years]. Nicephorus, Ecclesiastical History, book 12, chapter 34. In scarcely the space of thirty years he brought the Romans, the Persians, the Parthians, the Medes, the Indians, the Scythians, the Sauromatae, the Saracens, and indeed the whole human race under the yoke of truth, etc. Chrysostom, Homily 4, On the Praises of Paul. Clement, in his Epistle to the Corinthians, page 8, concerning the same: Κῆρυξ γενόμενος ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ καὶ ἐν τῇ δύσει, τὸ γενναῖον τῆς πίστεως αὑτοῦ κλέος ἔλαβεν δικαιοσύνην διδάξαι ὅλον τὸν κόσμον, καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ τέρμα τῆς δύσεως ἐλθὼν, καὶ μαρτυρήσας ἐπὶ τῶν ἡγουμένων, οὕτως ἀπηλλάγη τοῦ κόσμου [Having become a herald in the East and in the West, he won the illustrious renown of his faith, instructing the whole world in righteousness; and coming to the limits of the West and bearing witness before the rulers, he thus departed from the world].
gemini_english: Πᾶσαν σχεδὸν τὴν γῆν διελθὼν, καὶ ἐπὶ πέντε καὶ τριάκοντα ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ διαθλεύσας ἐνιαυτοῖς [Having traversed almost the whole earth, and having contended for Christ in the gospel for thirty-five years]. Nicephorus, "Ecclesiastical History", book 12, chapter 34. In the space of scarcely thirty years he brought the Romans, Persians, Parthians, Medes, Indians, Scythians, Sarmatians, Saracens, and indeed the entire human race under the yoke of truth, etc. Chrysostom, homily 4 on the praises of Paul. Clement in the epistle to the Corinthians, page 8, concerning the same: Κῆρυξ γενόμενος ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ καὶ ἐν τῇ δύσει, τὸ γενναῖον τῆς πίστεως αὑτοῦ κλέος ἔλαβεν δικαιοσύνην διδάξαι ὅλον τὸν κόσμον, καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ τέρμα τῆς δύσεως ἐλθὼν, καὶ μαρτυρήσας ἐπὶ τῶν ἡγουμένων, οὕτως ἀπηλλάγη τοῦ κόσμου [Having become a herald in the east and in the west, he received the noble glory of his faith, teaching righteousness to the whole world, and coming to the limit of the west, and bearing witness before the rulers, he thus departed from the world].
